title: Guided practice A: seasonal patterns
subject: science
phenomenonOrContext: Three years of monthly high temperatures at one town repeat the same yearly shape without repeating exactly, and a town in the south half of Earth records the opposite pattern in the same months.
lessonGoal: Use several years of weather records to find a typical season, and name the place it belongs to.
successCriteria: I use every year in the table, not just one.
I put the years in order, take the middle one, and say about.
I name the place a pattern came from.

vocabulary.definition: a part of the year with its own usual weather
weather someone measured and wrote down

sections.title: NOTICE — Three years at Riverbend
sections.body: Riverbend is an example town. Someone there wrote down the average high temperature for four months. They did it for three years. Read across one row at a time.

data.tableLabel: Riverbend average monthly high temperature, three years
data.note: Each number is the average high for that whole month. These numbers are an example made up for this lesson.

sections.title: NOTICE — What repeats and what changes
sections.directions: Use all three year columns. Pick the statement that fits every row.

items.prompt: Which statement describes the Riverbend records best?

choices.label: July is warmest all three years, and the July numbers are close.
July is exactly 83 degrees every year.
The numbers change, so there is no yearly pattern.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Close is still a pattern
sections.body: Read the July row: 83, 86, 81. Those are close, and July is warmest all three years. That is a pattern. Exactly 83 ignores two years. No pattern ignores all three.

sections.title: LEARN — Finding a typical number
sections.body: One year can be strange. Several years show what is typical. Typical means what usually happens. To find a typical number, put the years in order and take the middle one. Then say about, because the years are not all the same.

sections.title: MODEL — A typical July
sections.body: Watch how I find a typical July high at Riverbend.

items.prompt: Model task: find a typical July high at Riverbend.

steps: I read the whole July row: 83, 86, 81.
I put the three numbers in order: 81, 83, 86.
I take the middle one. It is 83.
I say about 83 degrees, because the years are not all the same.
My evidence is three Julys, not one.

sections.title: YOUR TURN — A typical January
sections.directions: Use the January row: 31, 28, and 34. Take the same steps I took.

items.prompt: Put the three Januarys in order. Enter the middle number in degrees Fahrenheit.
Which years did you use, and why do you say about instead of an exact number?

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Take the middle one
sections.body: In order, the Januarys are 28, 31, 34. The middle one is 31. Anything from 30 to 32 is close. Picking 34 or 28 uses one year instead of the middle.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Name your years
sections.body: A strong answer names all three Januarys: 2023, 2024, and 2025. They came out close but not the same. That is why you say about instead of one exact number.

sections.title: APPLY — The same July in two places
sections.body: Southpoint is an example town in the south half of Earth. Riverbend is in the north half. Both towns measured the same two months.

data.tableLabel: Riverbend and Southpoint monthly high temperature, 2025
data.note: Example numbers made up for this lesson.

items.prompt: What do these two records show?

choices.label: When Riverbend is warm, Southpoint is cool.
Both towns are warm in July.
Southpoint wrote its months down wrong.

items.prompt: A student says summer happens because Earth moves closer to the Sun. Use the two July numbers to show that cannot be right.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — One Earth, two seasons
sections.body: In July, Riverbend was 81 and Southpoint was 48. Both towns sat on one Earth, one distance from the Sun. One distance cannot make one town warm and one cool. You will learn why later.

sections.title: WHAT YOU LEARNED
sections.body: Several years of records show a typical season, so you say about. In the same month, the north half and the south half of Earth have opposite seasons.

sections.title: EVIDENCE YOU USED
sections.body: You used three years of Riverbend highs, the July and January rows, and the table that put Riverbend next to Southpoint.

sections.title: HOW YOU DID
sections.body: Your answers are saved and waiting to be checked. Watching me work out July does not show that you can do it.

sections.title: WHAT TO PRACTICE
sections.body: Practice two moves. Put the years in order and take the middle one. Name the place your pattern came from.

items.prompt: Why do three years of January records tell you more than one year does?
